title: Models and Simulations
summary: How computer models represent real systems in a simplified way, and how simulations use them to test predictions: inputs, rules and outputs, spreadsheet what-ifs, Goal Seek, simulations over time and chance, validation, and bias.

intro: A model is a simplified representation of a real system, and a simulation uses a model to test predictions before anything is built or spent. This topic covers abstraction, variables and data types, spreadsheet what-if models, Goal Seek and scenarios, simulations step by step and with chance, validating a model against real data, and asking who a model works for.

pages.spec: Explain what a model is, what a simulation is, and why people use them
pages.summary: A model is a simplified representation of a real system. A simulation runs a model to see what would happen, so people can test ideas safely, cheaply and quickly before trying them for real.

diagram.title: Who uses models?
diagram.caption: Match each model or simulation to what it is used for.
pairs: Weather forecast model
Predicts tomorrow's rain, wind and temperature
Flight simulator
Trains pilots to handle emergencies safely

Predicts the quickest route and arrival time

blocks.text: Before a new bridge is built, before a pilot flies a real passenger jet, and before the Met Office tells you to bring a coat tomorrow, someone has used a **[[model]]**.
What is a model?

A **model** is a **simplified representation of a [[real system]]**. It keeps the parts that matter for a question and leaves out the rest. A map of Enniskillen is a model of the town; a toy car is a model of a car; a spreadsheet that works out the cost of a school trip is a model of the trip.
In Digital Technology we are mostly interested in **computer models**: a set of values and **rules** (usually formulas or code) that represent how something behaves.
What is a simulation?

A **[[simulation]]** uses a model to **imitate what would happen** in the real system, often step by step over time. You change something, run the simulation, and watch the result. Simulations let us **test a [[prediction]]** without doing the real thing.

head: Model
Simulation
rows: A simplified representation of a real system
Running a model to see what happens
Formulas for how a cold spreads through a class
Running those formulas day by day to see how many pupils are off sick by Friday

blocks.text: Models all around you

head: Model or simulation
Who uses it
Why not just try it for real?
rows: You cannot test tomorrow's weather: you can only predict it.
Practising an engine fire in a real plane would be far too dangerous.
Closing a real road to see what happens would cause chaos.
Crashing hundreds of real cars costs millions of pounds.
Games model gravity, speed and collisions so worlds feel real.
You want to know if the plan is affordable before spending money.
blocks.caption: Everyday models and simulations

blocks.text: Why use a model?

items: **Safer**: crash a virtual car or fail a virtual landing and nobody is hurt.
**Cheaper**: changing a number costs nothing; building the real thing costs a fortune.
**Faster**: a computer can simulate years in seconds, or slow down something that happens in a split second.
**Possible**: some things cannot be tested for real, like how the climate might change over 50 years.
**Repeatable**: you can run the same test again and again, changing one thing at a time.

blocks.text: Engineers say: **model and simulate before you build**. Testing an idea on a computer first finds problems while they are still cheap to fix.

blocks.title: Worked example: model, simulation, or neither?
blocks.context: Decide for each: (a) a scale model of a new school building made from card; (b) a game that lets you run a virtual farm through ten seasons; (c) a photo of the school canteen.
steps: (a) A simplified version of a real building, used to see what it will look like: a **model** (a physical one).
(b) It has rules for crops, weather and money, and runs them season by season: a **simulation**.
(c) A photo just records what something looked like. It has no rules and cannot predict anything: **neither**.

blocks.text: A model is **never** the real thing. It is always a simplification, so its answers are predictions, not certainties. The weather forecast can be wrong!

blocks.title: Key points
items: A model is a simplified representation of a real system.
A simulation runs a model to see what would happen, often over time.
Models and simulations let us test predictions safely, cheaply and quickly.
Uses include weather forecasts, flight simulators, traffic, games and budgets.
Model and simulate before you build.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by a **computer model**.
practice.a: A simplified representation of a real system / situation (1) using values and rules (formulas or code) so it can be used to predict what happens (1).

practice.q: Give **two** reasons why car makers use crash simulations before building real cars.
practice.a: Any two: cheaper than crashing real cars (1); safer (1); faster to test many designs (1); can test the same crash many times / change one thing at a time (1).

practice.a: A model represents the system / is the set of rules (1); a simulation runs the model to see what happens, often over time / to test a prediction (1).

pages.spec: Use abstraction to decide what to include in a model and what to leave out
pages.summary: Abstraction means keeping only the details that matter for the question you want to answer. Every model also makes assumptions, and a good modeller writes them down.

diagram.title: The real canteen vs the model
diagram.caption: Abstraction keeps only what affects the length of the queue.

states.label: The real canteen
points: Hundreds of pupils with names, uniforms and moods
Noise, smells, trays, the menu board
Pupils arriving at slightly different times
Staff who sometimes chat or pause

states.label: The queue model
points: Time to serve one pupil: 15 seconds
Assumption: every pupil takes the same time

blocks.text: A real system has far too much detail to copy into a computer. If you tried to model *everything* about the school canteen, you would never finish. Instead, you use **[[abstraction]]**: you **remove the details that do not matter** for your question and keep the ones that do.
You may have met abstraction already, for example the London Underground map, which keeps the stations and lines but leaves out the real distances and streets. Every model is built the same way.
Start with the question
What you keep depends on **what you want to find out**. The same canteen could be modelled in different ways for different questions.

head: Question
Keep in the model
Leave out
rows: How long will the lunch queue be?
Pupils arriving per minute, number of tills, time to serve each pupil
Names, what they eat, colour of the trays
Will the canteen run out of pizza?
Portions made, how many pupils usually choose pizza
Is the canteen making a profit?
Price of each meal, cost of ingredients, staff wages
blocks.caption: Same canteen, three different models

blocks.title: Worked example: modelling the canteen queue
blocks.context: The principal asks: "If we open a second till, will the queue get shorter?" Which details should the model keep?
steps: Ask: does this detail change the length of the queue?
Pupils arriving per minute: **yes**, keep it.
Number of tills open: **yes**, it is the thing we want to change, so keep it.
Time taken to serve one pupil: **yes**, keep it.
Pupils' names, uniforms, the menu board: **no**, leave them out.
blocks.answer: Keep arrival rate, number of tills and serving time. Everything else can be abstracted away.

blocks.text: Assumptions

When you leave something out or simplify it, you are making an **[[assumption]]**: something you treat as true so the model can work. For example, "every pupil takes exactly 15 seconds to be served". In real life some pupils take 5 seconds and some take a minute while they find their money.
Always **write down your assumptions**. Anyone using your model can then see what it ignores, and you know what to check if its predictions turn out wrong.
Too simple or too complicated?

head: Too simple
Too complicated
rows: Leaves out something important, so predictions are wrong
So much detail it takes ages to build, run and understand
Ignores that half the pupils arrive in the first 5 minutes
Models every pupil's favourite food and walking speed
Slow, hard to check, and more places for mistakes

blocks.text: Leaving out a detail is a **choice**, and it can matter. A model of a school bus route that leaves out the pupils who live down narrow country lanes might suggest a route that is cheaper but leaves those pupils without a bus. Always ask: **who or what did I leave out?**
This is the same idea as **[[decomposition|Decomposition]]** and abstraction in computational thinking: break the problem down, then keep only what matters.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Abstraction means removing details that do not matter for your question.
What you keep depends on the question the model must answer.
Simplifying means making assumptions: write them down.
Too simple gives wrong answers; too complicated is slow and hard to check.
Ask who or what has been left out.

check.q: What is abstraction?
o: Adding as much detail as possible
Removing details that do not matter for the question
Copying a real system exactly
Breaking a problem into smaller parts
check.why: Abstraction keeps only the important details.

check.q: A model must predict the length of the lunch queue. Which detail should be left out?
o: The colour of the trays
The number of tills open
The time to serve each pupil
How many pupils arrive per minute
check.why: Tray colour does not change how long the queue is.

check.q: What is an assumption in a model?
o: A value that is calculated by a formula
An error found while testing
The question the model is answering
Something treated as true so the model can work
check.why: e.g. assuming every pupil takes 15 seconds to be served.

check.q: What is the main problem with a model that is far too complicated?
o: It always gives the wrong answer
It cannot use formulas
It is slow to build and hard to check
It leaves out too much detail
check.why: More detail means more time and more places for mistakes.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **abstraction** when building a model.
practice.a: Removing / hiding unnecessary detail (1) so only the details relevant to the problem / question are kept (1).

practice.q: A model is being built to decide whether the school car park needs more spaces. State **two** details that should be included and **one** that should be left out.
practice.a: Include any two: number of spaces (1); number of cars arriving / staff and visitors who drive (1); times of day cars arrive (1). Leave out, e.g., colour or make of cars / drivers' names (1).

practice.q: Explain why a modeller should write down the assumptions a model makes.
practice.a: So users know what the model ignores / its limits (1) and so the assumptions can be checked or changed if predictions are wrong (1).

pages.spec: Identify the variables, inputs, rules and outputs of a model and choose a suitable data type for each
pages.summary: A model takes inputs, applies rules, and produces outputs. The values that can change are variables, and each one needs the right data type: integer, float, string or Boolean.

diagram.title: How a model works
diagram.caption: Click each stage. Changing an input and running the rules again gives new outputs.

nodes.label: Inputs
nodes.detail: Values you can change, e.g. distance 18 km, average speed 40 km/h, 12 stops.

nodes.label: Rules
nodes.detail: Formulas or code that describe how the system behaves, e.g. time = distance ÷ speed × 60 + stops × 0.5.

nodes.label: Outputs
nodes.detail: The answers the model produces, e.g. journey time 33 minutes.

nodes.label: Decide
nodes.detail: Use the output to make a decision, or change an input and run the model again (a what-if).

blocks.text: Every computer model, from a weather forecast to a game, is made of the same four parts.

head: Part
What it is
School bus example
rows: A value fed into the model that you can change
Distance 18 km, average speed 40 km/h, 12 stops
A formula or instruction describing how the system behaves
Driving time = distance ÷ speed × 60; each stop adds half a minute
A value that stays the same every time the model runs
blocks.caption: The parts of a model

blocks.text: A **[[variable]]** is a named value that can change, such as *speed* or *number of stops*. Inputs and outputs are both variables: when an input variable changes, the outputs change too. That is the whole point of a model.

blocks.title: Worked example: the school bus model
blocks.context: A bus brings pupils 18 km to school from the far side of Lough Erne. Its average speed is 40 km/h and it makes 12 stops, each taking 0.5 minutes. How long is the journey?
steps: Rule 1: driving time = distance ÷ speed × 60 = 18 ÷ 40 × 60 = **27 minutes**.
Rule 2: stop time = stops × time per stop = 12 × 0.5 = **6 minutes**.
Output: journey time = 27 + 6 = **33 minutes**.

blocks.title: Worked example: change one variable
blocks.context: What if roadworks slow the bus to an average of 30 km/h? Everything else stays the same.
steps: Driving time = 18 ÷ 30 × 60 = **36 minutes**.
Stop time is still 12 × 0.5 = 6 minutes.
Journey time = 36 + 6 = **42 minutes**.
blocks.answer: Changing one input (speed) changed the output from 33 to 42 minutes.

blocks.text: Choosing data types
Each variable stores a particular kind of value, called its **[[data type]]**. Choosing the right one matters in spreadsheets and in code, because it decides what you can do with the value.

head: Data type
What it stores
Model example
rows: Number of stops: 12; pupils on the bus: 48
Time per stop: 0.5 minutes; ticket price: 2.75
Is it snowing? FALSE; Bus full? TRUE
blocks.caption: Data types in a model

blocks.text: Do not store a count of people as a float. You cannot have **48.5 pupils** on a bus! Counts of whole things should be **integers**. Money and measurements usually need **floats**.
A **Boolean** input is a great way to switch part of a model on or off. For example, *Snowing? = TRUE* could add 15 minutes to the journey using an IF rule.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Inputs go in, rules are applied, outputs come out.
A variable is a value that can change; a constant stays the same.
Changing an input variable changes the outputs.
Integer = whole number, float = decimal, string = text, Boolean = TRUE/FALSE.
Pick the data type that matches the real value.

o: Journey time in minutes

60 minutes in an hour

check.why: Speed is a value you can change and feed in.

check.q: What is a constant in a model?

practice.q: A model works out the cost of a pizza order. Identify **one** input, **one** rule and **one** output.
practice.a: Input, e.g. number of pizzas / price per pizza / delivery charge (1). Rule, e.g. total = number × price + delivery (1). Output, e.g. total cost (1).

practice.q: State the most suitable data type for each variable: (a) number of pupils on a trip; (b) cost per pupil in pounds; (c) whether a pupil has paid.
practice.a: (a) Integer (1). (b) Float / real (1). (c) Boolean (1).

practice.q: A bus travels 24 km at 40 km/h and makes 12 stops of 0.5 minutes. Calculate the journey time. Show your working.

pages.spec: Build a spreadsheet model with formulas and use it to answer 'what if' questions
pages.summary: In a spreadsheet model the inputs are cells, the rules are formulas that refer to those cells, and the outputs recalculate automatically. Changing one input to see the effect is a what-if question.

diagram.title: Try it: the Year 9 disco model
diagram.caption: Change the inputs and watch the profit. Costs are £150 for the DJ, £40 for decorations, plus snacks for each pupil.

blocks.text: Spreadsheets are one of the most common tools for building models, because a formula **recalculates automatically** whenever a value it uses changes. If you have studied the Spreadsheets topic, this page builds on it.
Example: the Year 9 Christmas disco
The Year 9 council is running a disco to raise money for charity. They need to know whether it will make a profit. Here is their model.

head: A
B
blocks.caption: Inputs in B1:B5, outputs in B7:B10

blocks.title: Worked example: checking the outputs
steps: Profit = 900 − 406 = **£494**, so B10 shows *Profit*.
blocks.answer: The model is working correctly: £494 profit.

blocks.text: Asking 'what if?'
A **[[what-if question|What-if question]]** changes one input and looks at the effect on the outputs. Change only **one** input at a time, so you know which change caused the difference.

head: What if...?
Input changed
Income
Costs
Profit
blocks.caption: Four what-if questions, one input changed each time

blocks.title: Worked example: only 120 pupils come
blocks.context: Snow is forecast and the council worries only 120 will come. What happens to the profit?
steps: Change B2 from 180 to 120. Nothing else changes.
blocks.answer: The disco still makes a profit, but £228 less than planned.

blocks.text: Never **[[hard-code|Hard-coding]]** values into formulas, e.g. `=5*180`. If the price changes, that formula will not update and your model gives the wrong answer. Always refer to the input cells: `=B1*B2`.
Colour your **input cells** (for example light yellow) and keep them together at the top. Anyone using the model can see straight away which cells they are allowed to change.

The DJ and decorations are **fixed costs**: they stay the same however many pupils come. Snacks are a **variable cost**: they go up with every ticket sold. Spotting which is which is a key part of building a money model.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Inputs are cells; rules are formulas that refer to those cells; outputs recalculate.
A what-if question changes one input to see the effect.
Change one input at a time so you know what caused the change.
Never hard-code numbers into formulas.
Label and colour the input cells.

check.q: In the disco model, which cell is an output?
o: B1
B2
B5
B9
check.why: B9 is calculated by a formula; B1, B2 and B5 are inputs.

check.q: Tickets are £5, 180 are sold, fixed costs are £190 and snacks are £1.20 each. What is the profit?
Why is =5*180 a poor formula for income?
o: It gives the wrong answer
Excel cannot multiply numbers
It will not update if the price or tickets change
It needs an IF function
check.why: Hard-coded values do not change when the inputs change.

check.q: Why should you change only one input at a time in a what-if?
o: Excel can only recalculate one cell
So you know which change caused the effect
Changing two inputs causes an error
It makes the profit bigger
check.why: One change at a time shows clearly what each input does.

practice.q: Using the disco model, calculate the profit if 200 tickets are sold at £5. Show your working.
Write the formula for cell B8 (total costs) in the disco model, and explain why it uses cell references.
practice.a: =B3+B4+B5*B2 (1). So the total updates automatically if any cost or the number of tickets changes (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between a **fixed cost** and a **variable cost**, using the disco as an example.
practice.a: Fixed cost stays the same however many come, e.g. DJ hire £150 (1). Variable cost depends on the number of pupils, e.g. snacks £1.20 each (1).

pages.spec: Use Goal Seek and scenarios to explore a spreadsheet model
pages.summary: Goal Seek works backwards: you choose the answer you want and it finds the input needed. Scenarios save whole sets of inputs, such as worst case, expected and best case, so you can compare them.

diagram.title: What-if vs Goal Seek
diagram.caption: Both use the same model, but they work in opposite directions.

states.label: What-if (forwards)
points: The model works out the output

states.label: Goal Seek (backwards)
points: You choose the output you want
e.g. How many must come to break even?

blocks.text: A what-if question works **forwards**: change an input, see the output. Sometimes you want to work **backwards** instead: *"How many tickets must we sell to raise £600?"* You could keep guessing, but Excel has a tool for it.
Goal Seek
**[[Goal Seek]]** finds the input value that makes an output reach a target. In Excel it is on the **Data** tab: **What-If Analysis > Goal Seek**. It asks three things:

head: Goal Seek box
Meaning
Disco example
blocks.caption: Goal Seek settings to find the break-even point

blocks.text: The point where income exactly equals costs, so profit is £0, is called **[[break-even|Break-even point]]**.

blocks.title: Worked example: the break-even point
blocks.context: Tickets are £5, fixed costs are £190 (DJ + decorations) and snacks cost £1.20 per pupil. How many tickets must be sold to break even?
steps: Each ticket brings in £5 but costs £1.20 in snacks, so each pupil adds 5 − 1.20 = **£3.80** towards the fixed costs.
The fixed costs are £190, so we need 190 ÷ 3.80 = **50** tickets.
Check: income 5 × 50 = £250; costs 190 + 1.20 × 50 = £250; profit = £0.
blocks.answer: Goal Seek gives 50 tickets: any more and the disco makes a profit.

blocks.title: Worked example: a target of £600
blocks.context: The council wants to raise £600. Use Goal Seek on B9 = 600 by changing B2.
steps: Need 3.80 × tickets − 190 = 600, so 3.80 × tickets = 790.
You cannot sell 0.89 of a ticket, and 207 tickets would fall just short, so **round up**.

blocks.text: Goal Seek often gives a decimal answer like **207.89**. For people, tickets or buses you must think about whether to round **up** or down. Rounding 207.89 down to 207 would miss the target.
Scenarios

A **[[scenario]]** is a saved set of input values that describes one possible situation. Planners often compare a **worst case**, an **expected case** and a **best case**. In Excel, **Data > What-If Analysis > Scenario Manager** stores scenarios and can produce a summary table.

head: Scenario
Tickets sold
Snacks per pupil
Income
Costs
Profit
blocks.caption: Three disco scenarios (ticket price £5, fixed costs £190 in each)

blocks.text: Even in the worst case the disco makes £160, so the council can go ahead with confidence. That is exactly the kind of decision a model is for.
A scenario can change **several** inputs at once, because in real life bad news often comes together: on a snowy night fewer pupils come **and** the shop may charge more for last-minute snacks.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Goal Seek works backwards from a target output to the input needed.
Set cell = output, To value = target, By changing cell = input.
Break-even is where income equals costs (profit £0).
Round Goal Seek answers sensibly, often up.
Scenarios save sets of inputs such as worst, expected and best case.

check.q: What does Goal Seek do?
o: Sorts the data into order
Changes several inputs at random
Finds the input needed to reach a target output
Draws a chart of the outputs
check.why: It works backwards from the answer you want.

check.q: Each pupil adds £3.80 and fixed costs are £190. What is the break-even number of tickets?
Goal Seek says 207.89 tickets are needed to reach a target. How many should be sold?
check.why: You cannot sell part of a ticket and 207 falls short, so round up.

check.q: What is a scenario?
o: A formula that works backwards
A saved set of input values for one possible situation
A chart comparing outputs
A single what-if change
check.why: e.g. worst case, expected case, best case.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a what-if question and Goal Seek.
practice.a: What-if: you change an input and see the output (1). Goal Seek: you set the output you want and Excel finds the input needed (1).

practice.q: Tickets cost £6, fixed costs are £190 and snacks cost £1.20 per pupil. Calculate the break-even number of tickets. Show your working.
Give **one** reason why planners compare a worst case, expected case and best case scenario.
practice.a: To check the plan still works if things go badly / to see the range of possible results / to plan for risks (1).

pages.spec: Carry out a simulation step by step over time and explain how changing a variable changes the outcome
pages.summary: A simulation over time applies the model's rules again and again, one time step after another, and each new row is worked out from the row before. Small changes to a variable can make a huge difference.

diagram.title: Test yourself: the sickness bug simulation
diagram.caption: Each pupil who catches the bug passes it to 2 new pupils the next day. Click a hidden cell to check.
head: Day
New cases
Total so far

blocks.text: Many real systems change **over time**: a population grows, a bug spreads, money in a savings account builds up. A simulation handles this by working in **[[time steps|Time step]]**: it applies the rules to get from one day (or minute, or year) to the next, then does it again and again. This repetition is a kind of **[[iteration]]**.
Example: a sickness bug in Year 9
One pupil in a year group of **120** comes in with a sickness bug. The model's rules are:

items: Each new case passes the bug to **2** new pupils the next day (the **spread rate**).
New cases today = new cases yesterday × spread rate.
Total so far = yesterday's total + today's new cases.

blocks.title: Worked example: run the simulation
blocks.context: Start on day 0 with 1 case. Work out each day until day 6.
steps: Day 1: new = 1 × 2 = 2; total = 1 + 2 = 3.
Day 2: new = 2 × 2 = 4; total = 3 + 4 = 7.
Day 4: new = 16; total = 31. Day 5: new = 32; total = 63.
blocks.answer: By day 6 the model says 127 pupils have caught it. But there are only 120 in the year group!

blocks.text: A result of **127 out of 120** shows the model has broken. Our rules forgot that pupils who have already had the bug cannot catch it again, so there are fewer and fewer people left to infect. Always ask: **does this output make sense in real life?**
Building it in a spreadsheet

head: A
B
C
blocks.caption: Spread rate (2) is stored in F1. Row 3 is filled down to make more days.

blocks.text: Each row uses the row above it, so you write row 3 once and drag it down. The spread rate is in **one input cell**, F1, with an absolute reference `$F$1`, so you can change it and the whole simulation reruns instantly.
Change one variable

head: Spread rate
Total by day 3
Total by day 5
What it could mean
blocks.caption: Changing one variable changes the outcome enormously

blocks.text: With a spread rate of 1, only 6 pupils have had it by day 5. With a rate of 3, the model passes the whole year group by day 5. This is why health experts focus so much on reducing how many people each case passes an illness to.
Real disease models used by scientists are far more detailed. They track who is healthy, ill and recovered, and they include randomness. But the idea is the same: rules applied step by step.
A spreadsheet chart of the *Total so far* column makes the pattern obvious: a curve that gets steeper and steeper. This is called **exponential growth**.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A simulation over time applies rules one time step after another.
Each row is calculated from the row before.
In a spreadsheet: write one row, store variables in input cells, fill down.
A small change to a variable can make a huge difference over time.
Check outputs make sense: impossible results show a missing rule.

check.q: In a simulation over time, what is a time step?
o: The total time the simulation takes
One jump forward, such as one day
The first row of the spreadsheet
A random number
check.why: The rules are applied once per time step.

check.q: New cases double each day, starting with 1 on day 0. How many new cases are there on day 4?
The sickness model said 127 out of 120 pupils were ill. What does this show?
o: The arithmetic is wrong
More pupils joined the school
The spread rate should be 3
A rule is missing, so the model has broken
check.why: Pupils who have had it cannot catch it again; the model ignored this.

check.q: Why is the spread rate stored in $F$1?
o: Absolute references calculate faster
Excel will not multiply by a number
So every row uses it when filled down and it can be changed in one place
So the spread rate changes on every row
check.why: The $ signs keep the reference fixed when the formula is copied.

practice.q: A model of rabbits on a farm starts with 20 rabbits. Each year the number of rabbits doubles. Work out how many rabbits there are after 3 years, showing each year.
Explain why simulations over time are often built in a spreadsheet by filling a formula down.
practice.a: Each row is one time step calculated from the row above (1); writing one formula and filling down repeats the rule for as many steps as needed without retyping (1).

practice.q: The sickness model predicted more pupils were ill than there were in the year group. Suggest how the rules could be improved.
practice.a: Add a rule that only pupils who have not yet had it can catch it / limit new cases to the number of healthy pupils left (1) so the total can never be more than 120 (1).

pages.spec: Explain why some simulations use random numbers and why they are run many times
pages.summary: Real life involves chance, so some simulations use random numbers. Each run gives a different result, so the simulation is run many times and the results are averaged to give a reliable prediction.

diagram.title: Chance of at least one six
diagram.caption: Change the number of dice rolls. The model works out the chance of rolling at least one six.

result.label: Chance of at least one six

blocks.text: Some things are not certain. A penalty taker does not score every time; it does not rain every day in Fermanagh (even if it feels like it). To model **chance**, a simulation uses **[[random numbers|Random number]]**.
Random numbers in a spreadsheet

head: Formula
What it does
Example result
rows: A random decimal from 0 up to (but not including) 1
A random whole number from 1 to 6, like rolling a dice
Gives Goal about 75% of the time
blocks.caption: Excel's random functions

blocks.text: These cells give a new value every time the sheet recalculates. In Excel you can press **F9** to force a recalculation and "run" the simulation again.
One run is not enough

Roll a dice 6 times and you might get no sixes, or three. A single run of a random simulation can be very lucky or unlucky. So we run it **many times** and look at the average or the overall pattern. The more runs, the closer the result gets to the true [[probability]].

head: Rolls simulated
Sixes
Fraction that were sixes
blocks.caption: One computer run (results change every time). The true probability is 1 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.167.

blocks.title: Simulating 1,000 dice rolls in Python
blocks.output: e.g. 171 sixes out of 1000 rolls. Run it again and you will get a slightly different number, usually somewhere near 167.

blocks.title: Worked example: penalty shoot-out
blocks.context: Ciara scores 75% of her penalties. A simulation of 5 penalties uses =IF(RAND()<0.75,"Goal","Miss") five times. Run 1 gave 5 goals, run 2 gave 3 goals. How many goals should the coach expect, on average?
steps: Two runs gave very different answers, so neither on its own is a good prediction.
On average she scores 0.75 goals per penalty.
Expected goals = 5 × 0.75 = **3.75**.
If the simulation is run 1,000 times, the average number of goals will be very close to 3.75.
blocks.answer: About 3.75 goals out of 5. Many runs give a reliable average; one run does not.

blocks.text: Weather forecasts do this too

The weather is very sensitive to tiny changes. Forecasters such as the **Met Office** run their weather model **many times**, each with slightly different starting conditions. If almost every run shows rain tomorrow, they are confident. If the runs disagree, the forecast is less certain. This is where a forecast like *"60% chance of rain"* comes from.
Do not judge a random simulation on **one run**. A single run that says "the team scores 5 out of 5" is just luck. Look at the results of many runs.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Random numbers let a simulation model chance.
RAND() gives a decimal from 0 up to 1; RANDBETWEEN(1,6) gives a whole number 1 to 6.
Each run of a random simulation gives a different result.
Run it many times and average the results.
More runs give a more reliable prediction.

check.q: Why do some simulations use random numbers?
o: To make the formulas shorter
To stop the results changing
To model events that happen by chance
Because computers cannot do exact maths
check.why: e.g. a penalty that goes in only some of the time.

check.q: What can =RANDBETWEEN(1,6) give?
o: Any whole number from 1 to 6
Any decimal between 1 and 6
Only the number 6
A number from 0 up to 1
check.why: It simulates rolling a normal dice.

check.q: Why is a random simulation run many times?
o: Excel needs several runs to start
One run might be lucky or unlucky
Every run gives the same answer
It makes the spreadsheet smaller
check.why: The average of many runs is a more reliable prediction.

check.q: A player scores 75% of penalties. How many goals would you expect from 8 penalties, on average?

practice.q: Write a spreadsheet formula that simulates a coin toss, showing *Heads* or *Tails*.
practice.a: =IF(RAND()<0.5,"Heads","Tails") or using RANDBETWEEN(1,2) with an IF (1 for the random part, 1 for the correct IF with both outcomes).

practice.q: A simulation of 10 dice rolls gave 4 sixes. Explain why this does not mean the chance of a six is 4 in 10.
practice.a: 10 rolls is a small number of runs, so the result can be lucky/unlucky (1). Running it many more times (e.g. 1,000) would give a fraction close to 1/6 (1).

practice.q: Explain why a weather forecaster runs the same model many times with slightly different starting values.
practice.a: Small changes in starting conditions can change the weather a lot (1); if most runs agree the forecast is confident, if they differ it is uncertain / it gives a percentage chance (1).

pages.spec: Test a model's predictions against real data and refine the model to improve it
pages.summary: Testing checks the model's formulas work as intended; validating checks its predictions against what really happens. If they do not match, refine the rules or assumptions and test again.

diagram.title: Validating a model
diagram.caption: Click each stage. If the prediction is not close enough, refine the model and go round again.

nodes.label: Predict
nodes.detail: Run the model, e.g. the bus journey will take 33 minutes.

nodes.label: Collect real data
nodes.detail: Time the real bus every day for a week.

nodes.label: Compare
nodes.detail: How far apart are the prediction and reality? Is the model always too high or too low?

nodes.label: Refine
nodes.detail: Change a rule or assumption, e.g. add 5 minutes for town traffic, then predict again.

nodes.label: Use
nodes.detail: Close enough? Use the model to make decisions, and keep checking.

blocks.text: A model is only useful if its predictions are close to what really happens. There are two different checks.

head: Testing
Validating
rows: Does the model do what I designed it to do?
Does the model match the real world?
Work out answers by hand with test data and compare with the spreadsheet
Compare the model's predictions with real measurements
Mistakes in formulas, e.g. a wrong cell reference

blocks.text: **[[Validation]]** means comparing a model's predictions with **real data**. The difference between them is the model's **[[error|Prediction error]]**.

blocks.title: Worked example: validating the bus model
blocks.context: The bus model predicts 33 minutes. A pupil times the real bus for a week: Mon 38, Tue 41, Wed 36, Thu 52 (heavy snow), Fri 37 minutes.
steps: Find each error (real − predicted): 5, 8, 3, 19, 4 minutes. The model is **always too low**.
Thursday was very unusual (snow), so look at it separately. The other four days average (38 + 41 + 36 + 37) ÷ 4 = **38 minutes**.
On a normal day the model is about 5 minutes short. Something is missing: the bus crawls through traffic in Enniskillen at 8:30.
Refine: add a new rule, *town traffic = 5 minutes*. New prediction: 33 + 5 = **38 minutes**.
blocks.answer: After refining, the model matches normal days. A Boolean input *Snowing?* could add extra time for days like Thursday.

head: Day
Predicted (old)
Real
Error
Predicted (refined)
blocks.caption: The refined model is much closer on normal days (times in minutes)

blocks.text: What makes a fair comparison?

items: Use **real data that the model was not built from**, so it is a genuine test.
Collect **enough** data: one day could just be a fluke.
Look for a **pattern** in the errors. Always too low? Something is missing.
Note unusual events (like snow) separately rather than ignoring them.

blocks.text: Do not change a model just to match **one** odd result. If you added 19 minutes to make Thursday fit, the model would then be wrong on every normal day.
Professional modellers do this all the time. Weather forecasters check every forecast against what actually happened, and this is one reason forecasts have become much more accurate over the years.
Each time round the loop (predict, compare, refine) the model should get a little better. This is the same **plan, build, test, refine** cycle used in all software development.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Testing checks the formulas work; validating checks the model matches reality.
Error = real value − predicted value.
A pattern in the errors points to a missing rule or a wrong assumption.
Refine the model, then test it again.
Use enough real data, and treat unusual events separately.

check.q: What does it mean to validate a model?
o: Check the spelling of the labels
Compare its predictions with real data
Add more formulas to it
Make the inputs a different colour
check.why: Validation asks whether the model matches the real world.

check.q: A model predicts 33 minutes; the real journey took 41. What is the error?
o: 8 minutes
74 minutes
33 minutes
41 minutes

check.q: A model's predictions are too low every single day. What does this most likely show?
o: The real data must be wrong
The model is perfect
Random numbers are needed
A rule or factor is missing from the model
check.why: A consistent pattern in the errors points to something the model leaves out.

check.q: Which is the best thing to do with one very unusual result, such as a snow day?
o: Change the model to match it exactly
Delete the whole set of results
Note it and consider it separately
Use it as the main prediction
check.why: Changing the model to fit one odd day would make it worse on normal days.

practice.q: Explain the difference between **testing** a model and **validating** a model.
practice.a: Testing checks the formulas / model work as designed, e.g. by comparing with hand-worked answers (1). Validating compares the model's predictions with real-world data (1).

practice.q: The disco model predicted 180 pupils. Only 152 came. Calculate the error and suggest **one** reason the prediction might have been wrong.
practice.a: Error 152 − 180 = −28 / 28 fewer pupils (1). Any sensible reason, e.g. bad weather, a clash with another event, assumption based on last year's numbers (1).

practice.q: Describe how a model can be improved after it has been validated.
practice.a: Look for patterns in the differences between predictions and reality (1); change / add rules or assumptions and then test it again against new data (1).

pages.spec: Evaluate the limitations, trade-offs and possible bias of models, including AI models, and ask who a model works for
pages.summary: Every model leaves things out, so it has limits. A model can be unfair if its data or assumptions leave some people out. AI models are models too: they learn patterns from data, so biased data gives biased results.

diagram.title: What went wrong with the model?
diagram.caption: Match each problem to an example.
pairs: Out-of-date data
A bus model still uses last year's timetable
Missing rule
A sickness model says 127 out of 120 pupils are ill
Biased data
Face recognition trained mostly on one group of people
Unfair assumption
Crash tests that only use a dummy the size of an average man
Too simple
A queue model assuming every pupil takes exactly 15 seconds
Garbage in, garbage out
A typing mistake enters 1,800 tickets instead of 180

blocks.text: The statistician George Box famously said: *"All models are wrong, but some are useful."* Because every model is a simplification, it will never be perfect. A good modeller knows the **limits** of their model and asks **who it works for**, not just whether it works.
Common limitations

items: **Missing factors**: abstraction left out something that turned out to matter.
**Assumptions** that are not true for everyone or every day.
**Data quality**: old, incomplete or wrongly typed data. *Garbage in, garbage out* (**[[GIGO]]**).
**The unexpected**: no model can predict every event, like a sudden storm or a pandemic.
**People change**: if a model says *"traffic is quiet on this road"*, everyone's sat nav sends them there and it fills up.

blocks.text: Trade-offs
Building a model always involves **[[trade-offs|Trade-off]]**: gaining one thing means giving up another.

head: Trade-off
One side
The other side
rows: Quick to build, easy to understand
More accurate, but slow and hard to check
Waiting hours for a better answer
blocks.caption: Trade-offs in modelling

blocks.title: Worked example: the disco price
blocks.context: A council member adds a rule: *for every £1 the ticket price goes up, 25 fewer pupils come* (300 − 25 × price). With fixed costs of £190 and snacks at £1.20, which price is best?
steps: The model says £7 makes the most money, but 75 fewer pupils come than at £4.
blocks.answer: Best for the charity: about £7. Best for pupils who cannot afford £7: £4. The model gives the numbers; people must decide what is fair.

blocks.text: Bias: who gets left out?
A model is **[[biased|Bias]]** if it gives results that are unfair to some groups of people, often because of the data or assumptions it was built on.

items: **Crash test dummies**: for many years the standard dummy was based on an average-sized man. Research has found that women are more likely to be seriously injured in similar crashes. In 2022, researchers in Sweden presented a crash test dummy based on an average woman.

**Exam grades in 2020**: when exams were cancelled because of Covid-19, a statistical model was used across the UK, including by CCEA in Northern Ireland, to work out grades, partly using schools' past results. Many pupils felt it marked them down unfairly because of their school's history rather than their own work. After protests, teachers' predicted grades were used instead (A level pupils kept the calculated grade if it was higher).

blocks.text: AI models are models too

An **[[AI model]]** is a model that has **learned patterns from a large set of data** (its **[[training data]]**) so it can make predictions or generate content. Like any model, it is a simplification, and it can only be as good as its data. If the data leaves some people out, the AI's predictions will be worse for them. For example, studies found some face recognition systems were much less accurate for people with darker skin, because they had been trained mostly on photos of lighter-skinned faces.
A computer's answer is **not automatically fair or correct** just because a computer worked it out. Ask: what data was it built from, what did it leave out, and who could lose out?

blocks.title: Key points
items: All models are simplifications, so all have limits.
Garbage in, garbage out: bad data gives bad predictions.
Modelling involves trade-offs such as simple vs accurate.
Biased data or assumptions can make a model unfair to some people.
AI models learn from training data, so they can carry its bias.
Always ask who a model works for, and who it leaves out.

check.q: What does garbage in, garbage out mean?
o: Bad input data leads to bad output
Deleted files can be recovered
Old models should be thrown away
Outputs are always more accurate than inputs
check.why: A model can only be as good as the data put into it.

check.q: Why were older crash test dummies a problem?
o: They were too expensive to use
They were made by computer
They were based on an average-sized man
They could only test slow crashes
check.why: Models based on one body type can be less safe for others.

check.q: How does an AI model learn?
o: A programmer writes every rule by hand
It copies a human brain exactly
It uses no data at all
It finds patterns in a large set of training data
check.why: AI models learn patterns from data, so their data matters.

check.q: A model shows the highest profit comes from a £7 ticket, but fewer pupils can afford it. This is an example of...
o: a missing input
a trade-off
a broken formula
random error
check.why: Gaining more money means fewer pupils can go.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **bias** in a model, and give an example.
practice.a: When a model gives results that are unfair to / less accurate for some groups of people (1). Example, e.g. crash test dummies based on men; face recognition trained mostly on lighter-skinned faces; 2020 grades model (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** limitations of using a computer model to make decisions.
practice.a: Any two: it is a simplification so may leave out important factors (1); assumptions may be wrong (1); depends on accurate data / garbage in, garbage out (1); cannot predict unexpected events (1).

practice.q: An AI system is trained to predict which pupils will do well at GCSE using data from only one school. Explain why its predictions might be unfair for pupils at other schools.
practice.a: It has only learned patterns from one school's pupils / training data is not representative (1), so it may not work for pupils with different backgrounds, subjects or circumstances / results would be biased (1).

pages.spec: Plan, build, test and evaluate a model of your own to answer a real question
pages.summary: Building a good model follows a cycle: plan the question, inputs, rules, outputs and assumptions; build it; test and validate it; then evaluate how well it works and who it works for, and refine it.

diagram.title: The modelling cycle
diagram.caption: Most models go round this loop more than once.

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Write the question, the user, the success criteria, the inputs, rules, outputs and assumptions.

items.label: Build
items.detail: Create the spreadsheet or program. Label and colour the inputs. Use cell references, not typed numbers.

items.label: Test and validate
items.detail: Check outputs against hand calculations, then compare predictions with real data.

items.label: Evaluate and refine
items.detail: Did it meet the success criteria? Who does it work for? Improve it and go round again.

blocks.text: Now it is your turn. Building your own model uses everything in this topic, and it follows the same cycle of **planning, development, testing and refinement** used to build any software.
1. Plan
Before you open Excel, plan on paper. A clear plan saves a lot of time later.

head: Plan section
Hot chocolate stall at the school Christmas fair
rows: What price should we charge to make at least £100 for charity?
Price per cup (float), cups sold (integer), cost per cup (float), stall hire (float)
Income = price × cups; costs = stall hire + cost per cup × cups; profit = income − costs
Same number sold at any price; no cups wasted; everyone pays
Profit is correct when checked by hand; answers the price question; inputs are clearly labelled
blocks.caption: A model plan

blocks.text: 2. Build

items: Put all **inputs together** at the top, labelled and coloured.
Write **rules as formulas** using cell references.
Format money as currency, and use sensible data types.
Add an IF output to make the answer obvious, e.g. =IF(B9>=100,TRUE,FALSE).

blocks.text: 3. Test and validate

blocks.title: Worked example: test with hand-worked data
blocks.context: Inputs: price £1.50, 120 cups sold, cost 40p per cup, stall hire £20. What should the model show?
steps: Profit = 180 − 68 = **£112**, so *Target met?* should be TRUE.
If the spreadsheet shows anything different, a formula is wrong.

blocks.text: Use **[[test data|Test data]]** that includes normal values, extreme values (0 cups sold) and values right on the target. With 0 cups sold the profit should be **−£20** (just the stall hire). After the fair, **validate** by comparing the model's prediction with what was really sold.
4. Evaluate and refine
An **evaluation** judges how well your model met its success criteria and what could be improved. Use evidence, not just "it works".

items: **Did it answer the question?** e.g. it showed £1.50 meets the target if 120 cups sell.
**How accurate was it?** e.g. predicted 120 cups, really sold 95.
**What were its limits?** e.g. it assumed the same sales at any price.
**Who does it work for?** e.g. could pupils with less money still buy a drink?
**Improvements**: e.g. add a demand rule, a scenario for a rainy day, or a chart.

blocks.text: Good project ideas: a canteen queue, your savings towards a new phone, a school sports day timetable, a fundraising event, the spread of a rumour through a year group, or a simple game with random dice rolls.
Do not write *"My model is perfect."* Every model has limitations. Naming them, with a sensible improvement, is what earns the best marks in an evaluation.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Plan first: question, user, inputs, rules, outputs, assumptions, success criteria.
Build with labelled inputs and formulas that use cell references.
Test with hand-worked answers, then validate with real data.
Evaluate against the success criteria, using evidence.
Name limitations, think about who it works for, and refine.

check.q: What should you do first when building a model?
o: Draw a chart of the results
Type the formulas into Excel
Evaluate the finished model
Plan the question, inputs, rules and outputs
check.why: Planning first saves time and mistakes later.

check.q: Price £1.50, 120 cups, 40p per cup, stall hire £20. What is the profit?
What are success criteria?
o: Statements used to judge whether the model does its job
The formulas used in the model
The assumptions the model makes
The random numbers in a simulation
check.why: You evaluate against them at the end.

check.q: Which is the best evaluation comment?
o: My model is perfect
My model works
It predicted 120 cups but 95 sold, as it ignored the weather
The colours look nice
check.why: A good evaluation uses evidence and names a limitation.

practice.q: A pupil plans a model of their savings for a £300 bike. List **two** inputs, **one** rule and **one** output for the model.
practice.a: Inputs, e.g. money saved already, pocket money per week, money from a part-time job / birthday (2). Rule, e.g. total = saved + weekly amount × weeks (1). Output, e.g. weeks needed / date they can buy it (1).

practice.q: Explain why test data should include extreme values as well as normal values.
practice.a: Extreme values (e.g. 0 cups sold) check the model still gives sensible answers at the limits (1) and can reveal errors that normal values do not show (1).

practice.q: Write **two** sentences evaluating the hot chocolate model, using the fact that it predicted 120 cups but only 95 were sold.
practice.a: One mark for using the evidence (prediction 120 vs real 95, so the model was too high / profit was lower than predicted) (1); one mark for a reason or improvement, e.g. it assumed the same sales at any price / did not include weather, so add a demand rule or a rainy-day scenario (1).

glossary.def: A simplified representation of a real system, used to understand it or predict what will happen.
The actual thing or situation in the real world that a model represents, such as the weather or a school canteen.
Running a model, often step by step over time, to imitate what would happen in the real system.
A model's estimate of what will happen. It may turn out to be wrong.
Removing details that do not matter for the question, keeping only what is important.
Something a modeller treats as true to simplify a model, e.g. every pupil takes 15 seconds to be served.
Breaking a big problem down into smaller parts that are easier to solve.
A named value in a model that can change, such as speed or number of pupils.
A value fed into a model that the user can change.
A formula or instruction in a model that describes how the system behaves.
A result produced by a model from its inputs and rules.
A value that stays the same every time a model runs, e.g. 60 minutes in an hour.
The kind of value a variable stores, such as integer, float, string or Boolean.
A data type for whole numbers, e.g. 12 stops.
A data type for numbers with a decimal point, e.g. 0.5 or 2.75. Also called real.
A data type for text, e.g. "Belleek route".
A data type with only two values: TRUE or FALSE.
Changing an input in a model to see the effect on the outputs.
Typing a fixed number into a formula instead of referring to an input cell, so the formula does not update.
An Excel tool that works backwards: it finds the input value needed for an output to reach a target.
Where income exactly equals costs, so the profit is £0.
A saved set of input values describing one possible situation, such as a worst case or best case.
One jump forward in a simulation over time, such as one day or one year.
Repeating a set of steps; in a simulation, applying the rules again for each time step.
A number chosen by chance, used in simulations to model events such as dice rolls.
How likely something is to happen, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
Checking a model by comparing its predictions with real data.
The difference between the real value and the value a model predicted.
Garbage in, garbage out: if the data put into a model is wrong, its outputs will be wrong too.
Gaining one thing by giving up another, e.g. a simpler model is quicker but less accurate.
When a model's results are unfair to, or less accurate for, some groups of people.
A model that has learned patterns from a large set of data so it can make predictions or generate content.
The examples an AI model learns its patterns from.
Statements used to judge whether a model or product does its job.
Values chosen to check a model gives correct results, including normal and extreme values.
